chunks.section: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
chunks.text: Xiaoran Chen 1,∗ Binghui Li 2,∗,† Liwei Wang 2,3,5,† Pinyan Lu 4,† 1 School of EECS, Peking University 2 Center for Machine Learning Research, Peking University 3 Center for Data Science, Peking University 4 Key Laboratory of Interdisciplinary Research of Computation and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics 5 State Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence, Peking University chenxiaoran@stu.pku.edu.cn {libinghui,wanglw}@pku.edu.cn lu.pinyan@mail.shufe.edu.cn

Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon’s preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast–slow momentum. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding authors.

Muon has emerged as a prominent alternative to Adam for training the matrix parameters of large language models (LLMs) ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its defining operation replaces a gradient or momentum matrix by an approximate polar factor, flattening its nonzero singular values before the parameter update. This matrix-level normalization offers a different way to allocate updates across directions from Adam’s coordinatewise rescaling. Recent frontier-model reports, including DeepSeek–V4.1–Flash ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) and Kimi–K3 ( Kimi Team and others, 2026 ) , adopt Muon variants for matrix optimization, with head-wise orthogonalization further adapting the update to attention structure. These developments make understanding when and why Muon improves learning an increasingly practical theoretical question.

Existing theory has established convergence guarantees for practical orthogonalization procedures ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ) and identified preconditioning benefits in structured optimization problems ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Full-batch associative-memory analyses further show how spectral normalization can balance learning across tasks with heterogeneous frequencies ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . In LLM pretraining, however, Muon acts on stochastic mini-batch gradients, and nonlinear normalization need not preserve the benefits predicted from population gradients. In particular, writing msgn \operatorname{msgn} for the partial polar map, generally 𝔼 ⁡ [ msgn ⁡ ( G t ) ∣ W t ] ≠ msgn ⁡ ( 𝔼 ⁡ [ G t ∣ W t ] ) \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{msgn}(G_{t})\mid W_{t}]\neq\operatorname{msgn}(\mathbb{E}[G_{t}\mid W_{t}]) . Recent work has begun to characterize stochastic spectral dynamics and geometry-dependent noise scales ( Paquette et al., 2026 ; Naganuma et al., 2026 ) ; the interaction between task occurrence, gradient reliability, and temporal averaging motivates the question we study here: Q1: When does Muon retain a directional learning advantage under stochastic gradient noise, and how do noise structure, batch size, and momentum determine this advantage?

Isotropic noise limits preconditioning. Standard stochastic optimization analyses often control gradient noise through a scalar variance bound ( Ghadimi and Lan, 2013 ) , leaving its directional structure unspecified. We use isotropic Gaussian noise as a diagnostic baseline. In the fixed-dimensional low-SNR limit, we prove that Muon’s conditional mean update is, to first order, a scalar multiple of the population gradient, as confirmed numerically in Figure 1 . SGD with a matched learning rate therefore reproduces this first-order mean drift: applying the partial polar map to each stochastic mini-batch gradient does not, by itself, produce directional preconditioning in the first-order mean response. Explaining such gains in this regime requires examining noise structure. Sampling controls balancing. We study associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies p j p_{j} ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Mini-batch sampling can leave task directions entirely unobserved; without momentum, Muon’s nullspace preservation then prevents updates along those directions. For two tasks, we prove an exact balancing threshold B bal B_{\rm bal} : below it, margins grow at unequal linear rates; above it, their gap has uniformly bounded exponential moments. For rare tasks, B bal ∼ ( log ⁡ 2 ) / p min B_{\rm bal}\sim(\log 2)/p_{\min} . In a higher-rank hierarchy, local perturbation estimates identify the expected task count B ​ p j Bp_{j} as a controlling scale. Experiments exhibit corresponding frequency-dependent crossovers, with frequent groups approaching balanced growth while rare groups remain occurrence-limited.

Label noise limits reliability. Label fluctuations persist at the population optimum, so frequent observation alone does not ensure a reliable gradient. Exact gradient statistics and a scalar projected counting model distinguish regimes governed by task counts B ​ p j Bp_{j} and corruption counts B ​ p j ​ ρ α Bp_{j}\rho_{\alpha} . Near the noisy optimum, an isotropic covariance closure with a locally homogeneous frequency approximation predicts a Muon contraction coefficient proportional to B ​ p \sqrt{Bp} , compared with SGD’s linear dependence on the local frequency scale p p . Orthogonal equivariance differs from coordinatewise sign updates. We use SignSGD as a proxy for Adam’s coordinatewise adaptivity ( Balles and Hennig, 2018 ; Kunstner et al., 2023 ) . Muon is orthogonally equivariant whereas SignSGD is basis dependent. In a two-task rotated sparse-support construction, a batch containing only the frequent task leaves the rare-task Muon margin unchanged but can decrease the corresponding SignSGD margin under certain conditions.

Momentum trades averaging for tracking. Momentum reduces sampling fluctuations, with frozen-state variance-equivalent batch size B eff = B ⁡ ( 1 + β ) / ( 1 − β ) B_{\rm eff}=B(1+\beta)/(1-\beta) , but longer memory introduces tracking lag. Under local tracking assumptions, the sufficient window η ≪ 1 − β ≪ B ​ p j \eta\ll 1-\beta\ll Bp_{j} motivates longer memory for rare, slowly varying directions and shorter memory where rapid tracking is needed. This provides a sampling-based perspective on curvature-conditioned multiscale momentum ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) : the local Hessian block p j ​ Γ j p_{j}\Gamma_{j} links rare tasks to low-curvature directions when label statistics are comparable. It also connects to occurrence-dependent forgetting in Activation-Keyed Momentum ( Hong and Qu, 2026 ) , supporting selective long-memory averaging as a means to improve estimates in slowly varying directions. Our contributions are threefold: • A diagnostic for stochastic directional gains. We prove a low-SNR expansion under isotropic Gaussian noise, showing that Muon’s first-order conditional mean response can be matched by learning-rate-rescaled SGD despite samplewise spectral normalization. • A theory of structured sampling. We establish an exact two-task balancing threshold and derive local higher-rank sampling estimates. With stochastic labels, we separate exact gradient statistics, scalar projected counting laws, and a square-root frequency prediction under isotropic covariance and locally homogeneous frequency approximations. A momentum-free Muon–SignSGD comparison isolates rotation-induced negative transfer under sparse sampling.

• A statistical basis for heterogeneous momentum. We characterize frozen-state variance reduction and local tracking error under temporal averaging, explaining when longer memory can help rare directions and providing a sampling-based interpretation of fast–slow momentum designs. Controlled experiments test these mechanisms, and a preliminary pretraining comparison illustrates their practical relevance.

Muon applies approximate polar normalization to matrix-valued momentum ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Existing work establishes convergence with Newton–Schulz iterations ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ) , preconditioning benefits in structured matrix problems ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and generalization gains from balanced learning on imbalanced data ( Vasudeva et al., 2026 ) . Magakyan et al. (2026) further identify scaling laws for momentum spectra and their implications for orthogonalization accuracy. For coordinatewise adaptivity, Li et al. (2026a) analyze SignSGD in feature-space linear regression, characterizing its loss dynamics and batch-size benefits relative to SGD. We complement these perspectives by studying how stochastic gradient structure governs Muon’s conditional mean response and distinguishes polar normalization from coordinatewise sign updates under sparse task sampling.

Paquette et al. (2026) characterize batch-dependent preconditioning regimes for Muon and SignSGD in high-dimensional matrix least squares. Naganuma et al. (2026) derive non-Euclidean gradient-noise scales for adaptive batch selection, while Eschenhagen et al. (2026) examine how stochasticity and temporal adaptation distinguish Shampoo from spectral descent. Our analysis focuses on random task support and persistent label fluctuations: we identify an exact finite-batch balancing threshold and separate task occurrence from gradient reliability. The isotropic Gaussian result provides a complementary fixed-dimensional diagnostic for the absence of first-order directional preconditioning.

Wang et al. (2026) connect Muon’s advantage over Adam to balanced learning of rare associations. Li et al. (2026b) analyze hierarchical task frequencies, label noise, and scaling laws through implicit matrix preconditioning. Beyond orthogonal embeddings, Kim et al. (2026) derive recovery and capacity scaling with Gaussian embeddings, including critical batch-size behavior. Building on the orthogonal associative-memory framework, we isolate finite-batch sampling effects through exact two-task dynamics and a higher-rank frequency-dependent regime map. Our SignSGD comparison further identifies rotation-induced negative transfer when tasks are absent from a batch.

Muon momentum has been studied as spectral filtering ( Li et al., 2026c ) , while activation-keyed and curvature-conditioned methods adapt memory across directions ( Hong and Qu, 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . We complement these designs with a sampling-based account of variance reduction and tracking lag.

We compare standard Muon with this fast–slow variant on a 0.12B-parameter dense language model trained for 30,000 steps, keeping the remaining training configuration fixed. Across all 138 shared checkpoints from step 2,600 to 30,000, the fast–slow variant has lower validation loss. Figure 6 shows the final 10,000 steps. Appendix H.8 documents the trajectory comparison.

We study when Muon’s preconditioning benefits survive stochastic gradient noise. Under isotropic low-SNR noise, its first-order conditional mean update matches learning-rate-rescaled SGD, showing that samplewise spectral normalization alone does not guarantee directional preconditioning. Structured sampling yields richer behavior: we establish an exact two-task balancing threshold and analyze higher-rank sampling effects governed by B ​ p j Bp_{j} . Label noise further separates task coverage from gradient reliability; an isotropic covariance closure with a locally homogeneous frequency approximation predicts square-root frequency dependence near the noisy optimum. A separate momentum-free SignSGD comparison highlights Muon’s protection against rotation-induced negative transfer under sparse sampling. Our momentum analysis connects frozen-state variance reduction with local tracking error, motivating longer memory for rare, slowly varying directions. This provides a sampling-based interpretation of heterogeneous momentum designs, supported by a preliminary 0.12B pretraining experiment in which fast–slow momentum lowers validation loss relative to Muon. Extending the analysis to evolving, non-orthogonal representations and validating these benefits across training scales remain important directions.
